summary.text: For \(n=67\), two distinct inputs give the same value: \(A049802(147)=1+3+3+3+19+19+19=67\) and \(A049802(2055)=1+3+9\cdot7=67\). Thus 67 occurs at least twice, so its occurrence count cannot equal 1.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
F(m)=\sum_{k=1}^{\lfloor\log_2 m\rfloor}\bigl(m\bmod 2^k\bigr)
\]
be sequence A049802. Thus A383327 is
\[
a(n)=\#\{m\ge 1:F(m)=n\},
\]
the number of indices at which A049802 takes the value \(n\). (Equivalently, in the bounded formulation used for this conjecture, one counts such \(m\) with \(0\le m<2^{n+1}\); the two indices below satisfy that bound.)

We disprove the asserted statement at the listed value \(n=67\). We will exhibit two distinct indices \(m\) for which \(F(m)=67\).

First take \(m=147\). Since
\[
2^7=128\le 147<256=2^8,
\]
we have \(\lfloor\log_2 147\rfloor=7\). The seven residues appearing in \(F(147)\) are
\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
k&147\bmod 2^k\\ \hline
1&1\\
2&3\\
3&3\\
4&3\\
5&19\\
6&19\\
7&19.
\end{array}
\]
Indeed, the first four values follow respectively from reduction modulo \(2,4,8,16\). For the last three, one may write
\[
147=4\cdot32+19=2\cdot64+19=1\cdot128+19.
\]
Consequently,
\[
F(147)=1+3+3+3+19+19+19=67.
\]
Thus \(147\) is one occurrence of the value \(67\) in A049802.

Now take \(m=2055\). Since
\[
2^{11}=2048\le2055<4096=2^{12},
\]
we have \(\lfloor\log_2 2055\rfloor=11\). Modulo \(2\), the residue of \(2055\) is \(1\), and modulo \(4\) it is \(3\). For every \(k\) with \(3\le k\le11\), write
\[
2055=2048+7=2^{11}+7.
\]
Because \(2^k\) divides \(2^{11}\) for all such \(k\), and because \(0\le7<2^k\), it follows that
\[
2055\bmod 2^k=7 \qquad(3\le k\le11).
\]
There are \(11-3+1=9\) indices in this range. Hence
\[
F(2055)=1+3+9\cdot7=4+63=67.
\]
Thus \(2055\) is a second occurrence of the value \(67\) in A049802.

The two indices are distinct, since \(147\ne2055\). Therefore the set
\[
\{m\ge1:F(m)=67\}
\]
contains at least the two distinct elements \(147\) and \(2055\), and so its cardinality cannot be \(1\). In other words,
\[
a(67)\ne1.
\]
If one uses the explicit finite counting range \(m<2^{67+1}=2^{68}\), both witnesses are still counted: indeed
\[
147<2055<2^{12}<2^{68}.
\]
Thus the same conclusion follows directly in that formulation as well.

Finally, \(67\) belongs to the set
\[
\{1,3,5,9,15,23,35,63,65,67\}.
\]
The conjecture claims that \(a(n)=1\) for every member of this set, and in particular would imply \(a(67)=1\). This contradicts the two distinct occurrences just constructed. Hence the conjecture is false.
